# Mahākapijātaka (Ja 407)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahākapijātaka* (Ja 407), also referred to in historical sources as the *Kapi-Jātaka*, is a canonical birth story belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon [Rahula 1956]. According to the narrative framework recorded at Jetavana, the Buddha preached the story to illustrate that doing good works towards one's relatives was a virtue he had practiced in previous existences. In the tale, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a magnificent monkey king ruling over eighty thousand followers in the Himalayas [Jones 2007; Taylor 2008]. When a human king and his troops arrived at their forest fruit tree, the Bodhisatta formed a bridge across the river with his own body so his troop could escape to safety, willingly sacrificing his life in the service of his subjects [Spink 2007; Wood 2005; Jones 2007]. In Sri Lankan historical tradition, this narrative of selfless service was preached by monks to inspire kings and local leaders to undertake public works, such as restoring reservoirs and monasteries [Rahula 1956].

The story is widely celebrated in early Indian Buddhist art. Art historians distinguish this tale of the "Monkey King" (Ja 407) from the other Great Monkey jātaka (Ja 516), which concerns an ascetic monkey who saves an ungrateful villager [Wood 2005]. Visual depictions of the *Mahākapijātaka* bridging the river or holding audience with the human king appear prominently on the railing medallions and uprights of the Bhārhut stūpa, on the gateways of Sāñcī, and in Cave V at Ajanta [Spink 2007; Seckel 2004; Wood 2005; Karlsson 1999; Shyu 2008].
